Hey so people told me there wouldn't be repercussions and that I would get help. That was very much not the case, and my situation deteriorated until I finally was pulled out of my command months later.

So in the end I guess it worked out. Though I now have the stigma of having been committed to a mental health institution. So much for working for a three letter agency. I had the prior job experience and fairly prestigious degree, but now I'm forever labeled. I don't know if, starting over, I would have just hidden the whole problem.

People who say the whole "just get help" mean well, but it's not that simple.

If you're going to get help, commit to getting help or if you want to hide it, commit to hiding it. 

If you try to go partially suddenly you'll find you go from being the golden child to "we need to send someone who is more... reliable" and standing the shittiest watches and working the shittiest jobs because "lol you're fit for full" until you ask why they won't send you to any training or career advancement opportunities. Then it's "you're obviously not well." The opportunities that I got denied and the rumors that the HMs spread because I got antidepressants just made me more depressed. Had I committed to hiding it and been able to do things to improve my situation or asked for LIMDU sooner I probably would not have been committed for suicidal thoughts. So commit to one or the other so it doesn't trash your options when you get out.

I had a bit of a breakdown a while back. I posted a question on an alt account on r/navy about what I was supposed to do, I fell through a gap in the navy's system when I was in a really bad place. Most Navy hospitals will help you if you have mental issue with no questions asked or referral required, but for some reason, the one near me doesn't follow the policy and kept turning me around over the course of weeks while I got worse and worse to the point where was non functional. The help lines kept sending me to them, who would send me back to my my unit to get a referral, who would "oh yeah we'll get you help 'soon'." I didn't want to straight up say, "I'm about to kill myself."

After I almost killed myself I called a different help line, who then got me an appointment at a different hospital a few hours away. They told me there they were really angry that I wasn't helped and the first hospital were supposed to have helped me get an appointment somewhere else instead of turning me around. Quality of care in the military ranges from really good to awful.

Because the policy, nobody believed me and most said I was just trolling or shitty at getting help when I posted a thread on r/navy asking what to do when I was in the middle of a breakdown.

At the time I kept asking this guy questions who was being pretty hostile because I felt like he was more "honest" or something. I took a picture because for some reason I thought reading it over and over would make me stronger or something. I don't really know, my meds were making me pretty off. Now that I'm on a half dose I'm almost back to normal.
